name: Question 1
problem:
The entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
equals $\frac{2}{5}.$ Find the value of $k.$
worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =2|\begin{aligned}k & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}4 & k \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(k-2)-3(4-6)+1(4-3k) \\  & =2k-4+6+4-3k \\  & =6-k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{12}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{12} & =(-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(4-6) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{21}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12} \\  & =\frac{1}{6-k}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{6-k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{21}^{′}=\frac{2}{5}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{6-k} & =\frac{2}{5} \\ 2\cdot 5 & =2(6-k) \\ 10 & =12-2k \\ 2k & =2 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the determinant of A:

det(A)=|2314k2311|=2|k211|−3|4231|+1|4k31|=2(k−2)−3(4−6)+1(4−3k)=2k−4+6+4−3k=6−k.

Since we want the entry a21′ in A−1, we need to know the value of c12 in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

c12=(−1)1+2|4231|=−|4231|=−(4−6)=2.

Then, since A−1=1det(A)CT, we have

a21′=1det(A)c12=16−k⋅2=26−k.

Finally, since we are told that a21′=25, we have

26−k=252⋅5=2(6−k)10=12−2k2k=2k=1.
